text: Lesson 21 chained dev, staging, and production together with needs — but a dependency chain only controls order. It says nothing about who, if anyone, has to sign off before a release moves forward. That's what promotion and approvals add: a real human checkpoint, enforced by the pipeline itself rather than a policy nobody reads.

Promoting a release means moving the exact same pinned artifact from one environment to the next, completely unchanged — nothing gets rebuilt, because rebuilding risks promoting something subtly different from what staging actually tested. What changes at each step is permission, not the artifact itself: does this specific release have the sign-off it needs to move forward.

In Azure DevOps, adding an approval to the production environment means any run targeting it pauses and waits. A named approver gets attached directly to the environment, and every future run targeting it inherits that same requirement automatically, with no extra configuration per pipeline.

Not every gate needs a person. A check is an automated condition — a business-hours restriction, a branch-control rule confirming the deploy only runs from main. Approvals and checks live in the same configuration panel on the environment, and a release can need both before it's let through.

When a run hits a required approval, it doesn't fail — it pauses, visibly distinct from running or failed, until the named approver acts. They review exactly what changed, then approve or reject with a reason. It never times out into a silent yes.

Getting sign-off to deploy is only half the story — approval just unlocks the door. Lesson 23 covers how that release actually reaches running pods without taking the application down — rolling, blue-green, and canary deployments.
